meta.coverage: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD, NZD, CAD, CHF · 28 pairs (full G10 ex SEK/NOK) + DXY + JPYBASKET + GER40 + EU50 + XAU + XAG + XCU + USOIL
meta.regime: Friday resolved both of the binaries this file was carrying, and it resolved them in opposite directions. Moody's declined to downgrade France - it kept Aa3 with a negative outlook and said explicitly that the review was not a rating action - which took the tail risk out of the euro, while the Strait of Hormuz escalation went the other way and lifted WTI 3.82% to 103.270 and Brent 3.14% to 116.720. The tell is what did NOT happen: gold fell 0.77% through 4,000 to 3,993.96, its first close under that level since July, silver fell 1.30%, and the Swiss franc was the single weakest currency on the board at minus 0.56% - on a day when a Houthi ballistic missile was intercepted over Riyadh and two supertankers struck mines near Hormuz. The market is pricing this as an inflation and supply shock that forces central banks to stay hawkish, not as a growth scare that pays havens, and the whole board follows from that one distinction.

dailyRead: This is a Saturday report, so everything here is Friday October 23 settlement and the weekend's news flow, and the week it sets up is the densest of the quarter. Start with what resolved. Moody's reviewed France's Aa3 negative rating on Friday evening and did not cut it - it affirmed Aa3, kept the outlook negative on the grounds that political fragmentation will continue to impair the functioning of French legislative institutions, and stated that the decision was not a credit rating action and not an indication of whether one is likely. Yesterday this file called that review the live binary and sized the euro short partly around it. It has now passed without damage, the OAT-Bund spread stands at 169.33 basis points against the 173.95 this file quoted on Friday morning, and the honest conclusion is that the euro got a tail removed rather than a reason to rally - which is exactly what the price did, with EUR/USD down 0.12% to 1.12022 on the day and down 0.31% on the week. The reason the relief did not pay is that the same session delivered a far more consequential euro negative. S&P Global's October flash PMI put the euro-area composite at 51.9 from 53.1 against a 52.7 consensus, a four-month low, with services at 51.7 from 53.0 against 52.5 expected and manufacturing at 52.4 from 52.9; S&P attributed the slowdown to rising energy costs and a sharp contraction in France, with Germany relatively resilient, and Chris Williamson put the signal at roughly 0.3% quarterly GDP. So France removed a rating risk and simultaneously supplied the growth problem, and the euro area is the most energy-import-exposed bloc in this file at a moment when European gas rose 4.23% on Friday to 93.86 and is 25.24% higher on the month. Second, the energy shock itself. WTI rose 3.82% to 103.270 and Brent 3.14% to 116.720, a third consecutive weekly gain and the highest since early May, with Brent now 9.49% higher on the month. The drivers are verifiable and they are supply-side: Houthi forces struck Saudi targets, with Saudi air defences intercepting a ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh early Saturday and destroying a drone over the Eastern Province, and the Houthis claiming hits on the Defence Ministry in Riyadh, an Aramco facility at Yanbu and the airports at Dammam and Abha; a maritime monitor counts at least ten ships hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, the highest tally since the war began; the IRGC claimed attacks on four vessels and said mines struck three more, including two supertankers; and the United States is enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports. Against that, the White House has said it will not attack Iran at any time before the November 3 midterms, Trump has publicly accused Iran of fabricating attacks to drive prices up, and Aramco says its production is not disrupted. The premium is real but it is political, and it can come out as fast as it went in. Third, and most useful for positioning, is the haven complex. Gold fell 0.77% to 3,993.96 - under 4,000 for the first time since July, down 4.14% on the week, 6.57% on the month and 7.54% on the year, which erases its 2026 gain - and silver fell 1.30% to 53.878, down 15.58% on the month. The franc was the weakest currency on the board, with USD/CHF up 0.56% to 0.82503 and EUR/CHF up 0.44%. The yen was flat at minus 0.06%. Reporting ties the gold move to two mechanisms rather than to indifference: an oil-driven inflation impulse that raises the expected path of policy rates everywhere and therefore real yields, and forced liquidation of a crowded leveraged gold long as the AI and semiconductor selloff generated margin calls, which is HSBC Asset Management's read. The US ten-year went back above 5% to 5.0010, up 4.4 basis points. That combination - war escalating, oil up four percent, gold and the franc down, yields up - is an inflation-shock regime, and it is why the board below is led by commodity currencies and why the two negative scores are a zero-rate haven and an energy importer. Fourth, the currency ranking itself. On the day: NZD plus 0.28%, AUD plus 0.16%, CAD plus 0.04%, USD flat, JPY minus 0.06%, EUR minus 0.12%, GBP minus 0.17%, CHF minus 0.56%. On the week the ordering is cleaner and more informative: AUD plus 1.24%, CAD plus 0.97%, NZD plus 0.80%, JPY plus 0.74%, GBP plus 0.38%, CHF minus 0.12%, EUR minus 0.31%. Fifth, two forward-looking shifts that are not in the price action and are the real work of this report. The first is New Zealand. This file has carried the kiwi at plus 1 on the arithmetic that an October 28 hike priced at 85-98% pays nothing on delivery and that the only downside was a trimming of that probability. On Thursday, speaking at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, RBNZ Chief Economist Paul Conway did exactly that: he said the late-October decision remains open, that policymakers want the flexibility to either hold the Official Cash Rate or raise it 25 basis points, and that while a hike is still the most likely outcome its timing is uncertain. He flagged oil gains and a weaker New Zealand dollar as near-term inflation pressures while maintaining that inflation returns to the 1-3% band next year. Separately, Wednesday's meeting is a Monetary Policy Review and not a Monetary Policy Statement, so there are no new forecasts to cushion whatever the Bank decides, and the expectation set is genuinely split - market pricing runs 80% to 98% for a hike to 3.00%, but ANZ expects no change and at least one published consensus has a hold. A near-fully-priced hike that the Bank's own chief economist declined to confirm, with no forecasts attached, is the largest two-way event risk on this board, and that is why NZD comes down to zero even though it was the strongest currency on Friday. It is a statement about the distribution, not about the kiwi's strength. The second shift is Switzerland, and it is the non-obvious call of the day. At its September 24 assessment the SNB held the policy rate at zero and dropped its earlier language about an increased willingness to intervene against franc strength, replacing it with a willingness to be active in the foreign exchange market as necessary, because haven inflows had receded and the franc had returned to pre-war levels; Bloomberg read that as the bank standing down from its war footing. The SNB raised its inflation forecast for every year to 2028, Schlegel declined to give a path, and he is reported to see the rate on hold until late 2027, with most analysts seeing no increase before 2028 even as markets price better than a 90% chance of the first rise by early 2027. Put that together with Friday: a currency with a zero policy rate and a 0.5030 ten-year - the lowest yield in this file - whose central bank has stepped back from defending it, which then underperformed every other major on a day of missiles over Riyadh. That is not a haven being paid, it is a funding currency, and CHF goes to minus 1. Sixth, the two currencies that improved. Australia has the least-priced hawkish path on the board. Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said in a speech that mounting evidence of rising global neutral interest rates raises doubts over whether policy is as restrictive as assumed despite four hikes this year - that he is confident policy is somewhat tight but questions whether it is tight enough, and that a higher neutral rate means the 4.60% cash rate may be exerting less drag than policymakers expect, which strengthens the case for keeping rates elevated or tightening further. Wednesday's Australian CPI at 00:30 UTC is expected to accelerate, with the monthly annual rate at 4.2% from 4.0% and the quarterly rate at 1.3% from 0.6%, and TradingEconomics carries 4.85% as its own end-of-quarter forecast against a 4.60% cash rate. The offsets are real and worth stating: the October services PMI collapsed to 47.8 from 51.9, manufacturing is 49.7, consumer confidence fell to 80.4 from 84.4, September employment fell 39,329 and unemployment is 4.7%, a five-year high, which Kent himself acknowledged. AUD goes to plus 2 on the strength of the pricing gap, not on the strength of the economy. The United Kingdom supplied the week's biggest upside surprise in the same release window that damaged the euro: the flash composite PMI rose to 53.1 from 52.0 against a 51.8 consensus, the highest since February, with services at 53.1 against 51.8 expected, manufacturing at 52.8 against 51.7, and employment returning to growth for the first time since September 2024. A November 5 hike to 4.00% is priced at 94-97%, the September MPC split 6-3 with three members already voting for it, and the gilt ten-year at 5.3656 is the highest yield in this file. GBP stays at plus 1 rather than rising, because that hike is now nearly fully priced and because the consumer side deteriorated sharply in the same week - GfK consumer confidence fell to minus 24 from minus 13 and September retail sales fell 0.4% against a minus 0.1% consensus. Seventh, Canada and Japan. CAD holds plus 2 and is the best-paid hawkish trade available: Brent at 116.720 is up 6.24% on the week against the roughly 75 dollars the Bank assumed in July, Wednesday's decision comes with a Monetary Policy Report, and TradingEconomics carries 2.50% as both the consensus and its own forecast while swap markets price only about 80% - so delivery still pays something, which is not true of New Zealand or Britain. The risk is not small: September employment fell 68.3 thousand after minus 41.7 thousand, unemployment is 6.5%, all three core measures are inside the band at 2.2%, 2.0% and 1.9%, Bloomberg's survey consensus is still a hold and one tracker shows 41%. Japan holds plus 1. Governor Ueda told parliament on Monday that underlying inflation is quite close to the 2% target, that it is increasingly important to anchor inflation around 2%, and - the tradeable line - that raising rates at an appropriate pace would help prevent spikes in bond yields, warning that failing to adjust could stoke concern about an inflation overshoot. The ten-year added 8.6 basis points to 2.7957 on Friday, the largest yield move on the board, September core CPI is 2.1% and the measure excluding fresh food and energy is 2.4%, and the October 30 meeting carries a fresh Outlook Report. The offsets are the energy import bill and Takaichi's proactive fiscal policy - a food consumption tax cut from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027 worth roughly 10 trillion yen with no explained funding, a 30-year JGB at a record high, and Washington pressing Tokyo to rein in spending to support the currency. At 156.865 the yen also sits inside the memory of the joint US-Japan intervention of late July and early August, the first since 1998, which cost a record 11.7 trillion yen in a month and came with an explicit promise not to hesitate to do it again. Eighth, the dollar. The Fed holds zero. A hold on Wednesday is priced near 93% and 94 of 100 surveyed economists expect it, while December 9 remains close to 90% priced - CME FedWatch on October 20 showed 9.6% unchanged, 75.2% for 25 basis points and 15.2% for 50 - so nothing in this file suggests the December repricing has unwound. The September projections had 16 of 18 officials seeing at least one more 25 basis point increase this year and four penciling in two, with PCE inflation at 3.7% for 2026 and unemployment marked down to 4.1%; Chair Warsh again declined to submit his own forecasts. The event is therefore the 18:30 UTC press conference rather than the 18:00 decision, and Warsh has already demonstrated this month that his words alone can cut October hike odds from 60-65% to about 15%. US third-quarter GDP, expected at 3.0%, and core PCE at 0.3% follow on Thursday morning. The cleanest trades follow mechanically from the scores and from which legs are least priced. Short EUR/CAD and short EUR/AUD are the purest expressions of the energy shock, pairing the bloc that pays for Brent and gas against the two that are paid for them. Short EUR/GBP at 0.83737, a seventeen-month low, is the single cleanest fundamental divergence of the day because one release separated the two economies. Long AUD/CHF has the widest score gap in the file and Friday proved its mechanism directly. Short USD/CAD is the best-paid single catalyst. Long AUD/NZD isolates the one antipodean divergence that Wednesday will actually settle, with the two events thirty minutes apart. The things to avoid are the pairs where both legs carry a near-fully-priced hike and an event inside five days: GBP/JPY, AUD/CAD and EUR/CHF are all levels trades this week, not direction. And the standing caveat on everything above is that the oil premium is political. A credible de-escalation headline, or confirmation that the White House means what it said about not striking before November 3, takes five dollars out of Brent quickly, and that single move would reverse the commodity-currency leadership, the gold short and the franc short at once. Not financial advice.

JPY.when: October 30 at 03:00 UTC, with a hold at 1.25% expected and hike odds put under 5%. The Outlook Report published alongside it carries fresh growth and inflation forecasts and is the actual event.

TradingEconomics carries 1.25% at quarter-end.

AUD.when: November 3 at 03:30 UTC. TradingEconomics carries 4.60% for that meeting but 4.85% as its end-of-quarter forecast, so its own model implies a move by December. Australian CPI on October 28 at 00:30 UTC is the input that decides it.
AUD.note: TradingEconomics verifies the cash rate at 4.60% after four increases this year. Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said in a speech that mounting evidence of rising global neutral rates raises doubts over whether policy is as restrictive as assumed - that he is confident policy is somewhat tight but questions whether it is tight enough, and that a higher neutral rate means 4.60% may be exerting less drag on demand and inflation than policymakers expect, strengthening the case for keeping rates elevated or tightening further. He cited persistent inflation, energy costs linked to the Middle East conflict and capacity pressures, noted household demand softening while business credit stays strong, and cautioned against over-reading monthly labour data while acknowledging that September employment fell and unemployment is 4.7%, a five-year high. Wednesday's CPI is expected at 4.2% annual from 4.0% monthly, with the quarterly rate at 1.3% from 0.6% and quarterly trimmed mean at 0.9%.

NZD.when: October 28 at 01:00 UTC, with the media conference at 02:00 UTC. Market pricing runs 80% to 98% for 25 basis points to 3.00%, but ANZ expects no change and at least one published consensus has a hold - the widest dispersion on this board.

This is a Monetary Policy Review rather than a Statement, so no new forecasts accompany it. The Bank's own prior assumption that a partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz had lowered oil and gas prices and eased near-term inflation has been overtaken by a 6.24% weekly rise in Brent, which argues the hawkish way even as Conway argues the flexible one.

CHF.when: December is the next quarterly assessment and a hold at zero is the clear expectation. Schlegel is reported to see the rate on hold until late 2027 and most analysts expect no increase before 2028, while markets price better than a 90% chance of a first rise by early 2027.

The SNB raised its inflation forecast for every year through 2028 while noting that rising energy costs and geopolitical tensions increase uncertainty, and Schlegel declined to offer any guidance on the path. September CPI is 1.0% and core 0.5%, both comfortably inside the 0-2% objective, so there is no domestic pressure to move. The asymmetry, if you want one, is that the BoC hike is better paid at 80% than Australia's November 3 meeting is positioned.

A hawkish RBNZ hike followed by a BoC hold is the full reversal, and Canada's minus 68.3 thousand employment print with 6.5% unemployment makes that less far-fetched than the swap pricing suggests.

symbols.why: At 112.01282, up 0.10% on the day - the oil pair, with Canada paid for Brent at 116.720 and a hike about 80% priced on Wednesday, against a Japan that pays for the same barrel and is expected to hold on October 30.

That two-sided event structure is why conviction stays low despite the clean thesis.

The franc is also the first thing bid if the Hormuz escalation becomes an actual closure rather than a risk premium, which would hit both legs of this trade at once.

Japan's fiscal position is the weaker of the two - a 10-trillion-yen tax cut with no explained funding against a record 30-year yield - and a BoJ that holds with unchanged forecasts sends this back up.

US third-quarter GDP at a 3.0% consensus and core PCE at 0.3% follow on Thursday.

The standing offsets are the energy import bill and Takaichi's unfunded 10-trillion-yen tax cut against a record 30-year yield.

An ECB that stays on hold without hawkish language on Thursday would also be a relief rally for the rate-sensitive part of the index.

Right now the French growth leg is dominating, which is why this is scored short and the DAX only lightly so; euro-area third-quarter GDP flash on October 30 at a 0.2% consensus is the confirmation or the refutation.

The Warsh press conference on Wednesday can also put real yields down in a single afternoon, and 4,000 is now resistance that was support.

symbols.risk: Silver's float is small enough that a squeeze can run against the fundamentals for days, so size this smaller than the gold short. A Hormuz closure would take both metals up together, and any sign that the AI capital-spending scare is over restores the industrial leg immediately.

symbols.why: At 6.4760 dollars per pound, up 1.78% on the day but down 0.84% on the week and 3.69% on the month while 13.97% higher on the year; the physical read is genuinely two-sided - LME available stocks hit a two-month high around 147,450 tonnes and COMEX now trades below LME, reversing July's tariff premium, while Chinese buyers pay the largest import premium since 2022 at about 118 dollars over LME.
symbols.risk: Tie it to AUD, which it supported on Friday. The refined-copper tariff is still unimplemented and a decision either way is a gap, Goldman reads the US inventory as stranded supply rather than genuine tightness while Citi targets 15,000 dollars a tonne within twelve months, and Australian CPI on Wednesday is the event for the correlation leg.

Keep this consistent with the CAD long, since both rest on the same barrel.

catalysts.event: Canada: September CPI m/m, Median CPI y/y and Trimmed CPI y/y (Statistics Canada red folder)
catalysts.note: The last Canadian inflation print before the October 28 decision. TradingEconomics carries September CPI at 3.1% from 3.0% with core down to 2.2%, Median at 2.0% and Trimmed at 1.9% - all three core measures inside the band while the headline is not. That split is what StoneX cited as giving the Bank room to hold, and it is why Canadian pricing remains the least uniform of the hawkish meetings, with swaps near 80%, BMO, RBC and Desjardins at 2.50%, Bloomberg's survey consensus still at a hold and one tracker at 41%.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: September CPI y/y (ONS red folder)
catalysts.note: Released above forecast at 3.5% year on year against a 3.4% consensus and 3.1% in August, carried on TradingEconomics, with core matching consensus at 2.8% from 2.6% and services inflation accelerating to 3.7% from 3.4%. Motor fuel 29.8% higher than a year earlier did the work, which is the oil premium arriving in the UK index rather than fresh domestic pressure. Combined with Friday's composite PMI at 53.1 it has left the November 5 hike to 4.00% priced at 94-97%, while December 17 remains the open question - one year-end path implies 4.00% and therefore no second increase.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 CPI q/q (Stats NZ red folder)
catalysts.note: Released below forecast at 0.7% q/q against a 0.8% consensus and 1.5% in Q2, with the annual rate at 3.7% from 4.1% against 3.8% expected - both verified on TradingEconomics. It was the most dovish outcome available, two tenths under the RBNZ's own 3.9% projection, with cheaper petrol and diesel taking roughly 0.4 percentage points off the quarterly pace. Pricing for October 28 nonetheless held at 80% to 98% because 3.7% is still outside the 1-3% band - and then the Bank's own chief economist reopened the decision on Thursday.

catalysts.event: Japan: National Core CPI y/y (Statistics Bureau)
catalysts.note: Core inflation printed 2.1% against 1.7% in August, matching consensus and clearing the Bank of Japan's 2% target for the first time since December; headline rose to 2.1% from 1.9% and the narrow measure excluding fresh food and energy jumped to 2.4% from 1.9%, all verified on TradingEconomics, which also carries inflation expectations at 3.5% from 2.7%. Governor Ueda had told parliament on Monday that underlying inflation was quite close to target; the 2.4% figure says it has arrived. The market reaction was muted at the time because swaps already priced December heavily and no analyst expects a move on October 30 - but the JGB ten-year then added 8.6 basis points on Friday.

catalysts.event: Euro area: HCOB flash composite, services and manufacturing PMI for October (S&P Global)
catalysts.note: The most consequential euro negative of the week and a clear miss on every line. The composite fell to 51.9 from 53.1 against a 52.7 consensus, a four-month low; services dropped to 51.7 from 53.0 against 52.5 expected; manufacturing eased to 52.4 from 52.9 against 52.7. S&P Global attributed the slowdown to rising energy costs and a sharp contraction in France, with Germany showing relative resilience, and Chris Williamson put the signal at roughly 0.3% quarterly GDP growth. This is the oil and gas shock arriving as a euro-area growth problem, with European gas up 25.24% on the month, and it is why the Moody's relief on France produced no euro bid.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: S&P Global flash composite, services and manufacturing PMI for October
catalysts.note: The week's biggest upside surprise, and it landed in the same window as the euro-area miss. The composite rose to 53.1 from 52.0 against a 51.8 consensus, the highest since February; services printed 53.1 against 51.8 expected and manufacturing 52.8 against 51.7, both verified on TradingEconomics. Employment returned to growth for the first time since September 2024. S&P Global's chief business economist said the persistent price pressures are likely to prompt a Bank of England hike on November 5. EUR/GBP extended to a seventeen-month low at 0.83737 on the divergence, which is the cleanest single-release fundamental split on this board.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: September retail sales m/m (ONS)
catalysts.note: Released below forecast at minus 0.4% m/m against a minus 0.1% consensus and 0.7% in August, with the annual rate at 1.0% against 1.3% expected, carried on TradingEconomics. Taken with GfK consumer confidence collapsing to minus 24 from minus 13 in October, this is the counterweight to the PMI beat and the specific reason sterling holds at plus 1 rather than rising: the business survey is the strongest since February while the household data is deteriorating fast, and a hawkish repricing with a broken consumer behind it is the kind that stalls.

catalysts.event: France: Moody's scheduled review of the Aa3 negative rating
catalysts.note: Resolved without damage. Moody's affirmed France at Aa3, kept the outlook negative on the grounds that political fragmentation will continue to impair the functioning of French legislative institutions, and stated explicitly that the decision was not a credit rating action and not an indication of whether one is likely in the near future. Fitch and S&P both rate France lower, at A plus since 2025. The OAT-Bund spread stands at 169.33 basis points with the OAT ten-year at 5.0367 against a 3.3434 Bund. The tail risk this file carried into the weekend is gone, but the relief removed a threat rather than creating a bid - which is precisely what the euro's minus 0.12% session showed.

catalysts.event: United States: September durable goods orders m/m
catalysts.note: The last US data of consequence before the Fed, with consensus at 0.6% from 0.0% and TradingEconomics at 0.4%. It matters mainly as a read on whether the capital-spending cycle that is driving the AI story is still intact after a week in which the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 6.72% in a session and the Nasdaq lost 2.60%. A strong number keeps the December hike near 90% priced; a weak one gives Chair Warsh cover to sound cautious the following afternoon.

catalysts.event: Australia: September monthly CPI y/y, quarterly CPI and RBA trimmed mean (ABS red folder)
catalysts.note: The first of four central-bank-relevant events in eighteen hours and the decisive input for the November 3 RBA. Consensus has the monthly annual rate accelerating to 4.2% from 4.0% with TradingEconomics at 4.1%, the quarterly rate at 1.3% from 0.6%, the monthly trimmed mean at 0.3% from 0.2% and the quarterly trimmed mean at 0.9% from 0.8% with the annual trimmed mean at 3.5-3.6%. TradingEconomics carries 4.85% as its end-of-quarter cash rate forecast against 4.60% now. This is the print that decides whether Assistant Governor Kent's argument that 4.60% may not be tight enough becomes policy, and it lands thirty minutes before the RBNZ.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review and OCR decision (red folder)
catalysts.note: The largest two-way event risk on this board. Market pricing runs 80% to 98% for a 25 basis point hike to 3.00%, but Chief Economist Paul Conway said on Thursday in Bangkok that the decision remains open and that policymakers want the flexibility to either hold or raise, with a hike still most likely but its timing uncertain; ANZ expects no change and at least one published consensus has a hold. This is a Review rather than a Statement, so no new forecasts accompany it - there is nothing to cushion the message either way. Watch whether the statement marks up the Q4 track, where economists see the annual rate back above 4% against the Bank's own 3.9%, and whether it abandons the prior assumption that a partial Hormuz reopening had eased oil and gas prices.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ online media conference
catalysts.note: An hour after the decision, and more important than usual precisely because the Review publishes no forecasts - the words are the only guidance available. With Conway having already put a hold on the table, the question is whether Governor and committee confirm a continued tightening path or present the move, if it comes, as the last of the cycle. A delivered hike framed as sufficient would be dovish at this level of pricing; an explicit signal of more to come is the only configuration that pays a long kiwi.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada rate decision and Monetary Policy Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: The best-paid catalyst in this file. TradingEconomics carries 2.50% as both the market consensus and its own forecast, up from 2.25%, with swaps near 80%, BMO, RBC and Desjardins having moved to a hike - against Bloomberg's survey consensus still at a hold and one tracker at 41%. That dispersion is the point: unlike New Zealand at up to 98% or Britain at 94-97%, a delivered Canadian hike still repays. The MPR published alongside it will carry the Bank's new oil assumption, which matters because Brent at 116.720 is 6.24% higher on the week against the roughly 75 dollars assumed in July. The case against remains the labour market at minus 68.3 thousand jobs and 6.5% unemployment with all three core measures inside the band.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada press conference
catalysts.note: Forty-five minutes after the decision and three and a half hours before the Fed. Governor Macklem's October 17 argument that the energy shock is feeding through to inflation expectations is what moved swap pricing from about 30% to 80% in a week, so the question is whether he validates a hike as the start of a sequence or as a one-off insurance move against the war premium. A hike presented as sufficient, with the MPR assuming oil eases, would take much of the loonie's remaining upside away even on delivery.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC rate decision (red folder)
catalysts.note: A hold at 3.75-4.00% is priced near 93% with hike odds around 7%, and 94 of 100 surveyed economists expect no change; TradingEconomics carries 4.00% for the meeting. The decision itself is therefore close to a non-event and the entire interest is in what it says about December 9, which remains near 90% priced - CME FedWatch on October 20 split 9.6% unchanged, 75.2% for 25 basis points and 15.2% for 50. The September projections had 16 of 18 officials seeing at least one more increase this year and four penciling in two, with PCE inflation at 3.7% for 2026 and unemployment marked down to 4.1%. Watch the statement language on energy pass-through, since that is the mechanism now driving every other bank in this file.

catalysts.event: United States: Fed press conference with Chair Warsh
catalysts.note: The single largest two-way risk of the week for every dollar leg on this board, and the reason DXY is scored RANGE rather than directionally. Warsh has already demonstrated this month that his comments alone can cut October hike odds from 60-65% to roughly 15%, and he again declined to submit his own forecasts to the September projections - so he is under no obligation to defend the committee's dots or the 90%-priced December. A chair who leans on the oil shock as transitory defuses December and reverses the dollar legs of EUR/USD, USD/CHF and USD/JPY at once; one who endorses the dots validates them.

catalysts.event: United States: Q3 GDP advance and September core PCE price index m/m (red folder)
catalysts.note: Both land at the same minute, the morning after the Fed, with GDP consensus at 3.0% quarterly from 2.2% and TradingEconomics at 3.1%, and core PCE at 0.3% from 0.2%. Personal income and personal spending print alongside, at 0.3% each against 0.2% and 0.9%. Core PCE is the Fed's own target measure and this is the last reading before December 9, so a 0.4% surprise would put the 50 basis point bucket - currently 15.2% on FedWatch - back in play, while a 0.2% print with a strong GDP number is the combination that lets the committee wait.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB rate decision and deposit facility rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: A hold at a 2.50% deposit rate and 2.65% main refinancing rate is expected by 70 of 73 economists in a Reuters poll, and TradingEconomics carries both as its own forecast for the meeting while projecting 2.90% refi - implying 2.75% deposit - by end of quarter. So the decision is about December, not October. The September meeting delivered the second hike since the war began, kept 2026 inflation at 3.0% and revised 2027 up to 2.5% and 2028 to 2.1%, while upgrading growth to 0.9% for 2026. Friday's flash PMI at a four-month low on energy costs and a French contraction is the new information the Council has to absorb.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB press conference with President Lagarde
catalysts.note: The field most likely to change the euro's rate path this week. Lagarde's September formulation was that risks to growth are tilted to the downside while inflation risks are tilted to the upside, decided meeting by meeting - and Friday handed her fresh evidence for the growth half, with the composite at 51.9 and France contracting sharply. A Lagarde who leans on 3.8% headline inflation and the upgraded 2027 track keeps December alive and would squeeze a euro short that is now consensus; one who leads with the PMI and the energy drag confirms the minus 1 score. The OAT-Bund spread at 169.33 basis points and the Moody's affirmation give her one less problem to manage.

catalysts.event: Japan: Bank of Japan rate decision and Outlook Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: A hold at 1.25% is expected with hike odds put under 5%, so the Outlook Report's fresh growth and inflation forecasts are the event. Ueda has given the hawkish setup himself: underlying inflation quite close to 2%, anchoring it around 2% increasingly important, and raising rates at an appropriate pace as a way to prevent spikes in bond yields - with failure to adjust risking an inflation overshoot. September core CPI is 2.1% and the measure excluding fresh food and energy is 2.4%, and the ten-year added 8.6 basis points on Friday. An upgraded inflation track is what a long yen needs; unchanged forecasts send USD/JPY back toward 158.

catalysts.event: Euro area: Q3 GDP growth rate flash, q/q and y/y
catalysts.note: Consensus has quarterly growth decelerating to 0.2% from 0.6%, with TradingEconomics at 0.1%, and the annual rate at 1.1% from 1.2%. The day after the ECB, this either confirms or refutes the message of Friday's flash PMI - Williamson read the survey as consistent with roughly 0.3% quarterly growth, so a 0.1% print would be worse than even the weakened survey implied. It is also the cleanest scheduled test of the EU50 short, since French and Italian national figures publish the same morning and France is the index's second-largest country weight.

catalysts.event: United States: ISM manufacturing PMI for October
catalysts.note: Previous 54.5, with the S&P Global flash already at 56.0 for October against 55.9. The series matters more than usual because it is the first hard read on whether the energy shock is reaching US input costs and prices paid, which is the channel that would make the December hike a 50 basis point question rather than a 25 one. The prices-paid subindex is the line to watch rather than the headline.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA rate decision (red folder)
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics carries 4.60% for the meeting but 4.85% as its end-of-quarter forecast, so its own model implies a move by December. The hawkish case is Assistant Governor Kent's: rising global neutral rates mean a 4.60% cash rate may be exerting less drag than assumed, which argues for keeping rates elevated or tightening further regardless of the next data point. The case against is the domestic deterioration - October services PMI at 47.8 from 51.9, manufacturing at 49.7, consumer confidence at 80.4, September employment down 39,329 and unemployment at a five-year high of 4.7%. Wednesday's CPI decides which argument the Board leads with.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA press conference
catalysts.note: An hour after the decision and the place where the neutral-rate argument either becomes the Board's framework or stays one assistant governor's speech. If the Governor adopts Kent's reasoning that policy may not be tight enough despite four hikes, the Australian path reprices hawkishly on a view rather than on data, which is what makes AUD the least-priced long on this board. US midterm elections fall the same day, which is also the date the White House has tied to its commitment not to strike Iran.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: Bank of England rate decision, Monetary Policy Summary and vote split (red folder)
catalysts.note: A 25 basis point hike to 4.00% is priced at 94-97%, which is as close to settled as anything in this file, after the September MPC split 6-3 with three members already voting for exactly that. With the move effectively paid for, the tradeable content is the vote split and whether the Committee signals a second increase: one published year-end path implies 4.00% and therefore nothing at December 17. catalysts.event: Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure
catalysts.note: The live variable behind every score in this file and the only one with no scheduled time. At least ten vessels have been hit in or near the Strait since Sunday, the highest count since the war began, with the IRGC claiming attacks on four ships and mines striking three more including two supertankers; Saudi air defences intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh early Saturday and the Houthis claim hits on the Defence Ministry, the Aramco facility at Yanbu and the Dammam and Abha airports, with Aramco evacuating staff. Reports say Washington and Israel are preparing renewed large-scale strikes, while the White House has said it will not attack Iran at any time before the November 3 midterms and Trump has accused Iran of fabricating attacks to lift prices. Aramco says production is undisrupted. The distinction that matters for positioning is premium versus closure: a premium is hawkish and keeps this board as it stands, a closure is a growth shock that reverses the gold short, the franc short and the commodity-currency leadership together.

geopolitics: The transmission chain from the Gulf to this board is now the single organising fact of the report, and Friday clarified exactly which link is loaded. On the supply side the escalation is verifiable and it accelerated: a maritime monitor counts at least ten ships hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Sunday, the highest tally since the war began, with vessels exposed to indiscriminate attack even when they switch off tracking; the IRGC claimed strikes on four vessels and said mines hit three more, including two supertankers, along the southern route hugging the Omani coast that the United States uses to escort tankers out of the Gulf; the US is enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports; and the Houthis took the war to Saudi energy and defence infrastructure, with Saudi air defences intercepting a ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh early Saturday and destroying a drone over the Eastern Province, while the Houthis claim hits on the Defence Ministry in Riyadh, the Aramco facility at Yanbu and the airports at Dammam and Abha. Aramco has evacuated staff. Reporting also says Washington and Israel are preparing renewed large-scale strikes with additional forces moving to the region. The price response was immediate and large: WTI up 3.82% to 103.270, Brent up 3.14% to 116.720 and a third consecutive weekly gain to the highest since early May, European gas up 4.23% to 93.86, German gas up 4.21% to 95.15 and UK gas up 3.99% to 230.84. On the month Brent is 9.49% higher, European gas 25.24% and German gas 24.85%. Against all of that sit three genuine counterweights that stop this being a one-way premium: the White House has stated that the United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the November 3 midterm elections, Trump has publicly accused Iran of fabricating strikes, mines and everything else in order to drive oil prices up, and Saudi Aramco says its production has not been disrupted. Some analysts therefore place any renewed strike campaign after November 3, though one US envoy suggested an attack could come over the weekend, and the sources genuinely conflict. The FX read is where Friday was most instructive, and it rests on one distinction: is this a supply shock or a growth shock. The market answered clearly. Gold fell 0.77% through 4,000 to 3,993.96 - its first close below that level since July, down 4.14% on the week and 7.54% on the year, which erases the 2026 gain - silver fell 1.30%, the Swiss franc was the weakest currency on the board at minus 0.56%, the yen was flat, and the US ten-year went back above 5% to 5.0010. Havens did not get paid during an escalation. That is the behaviour of a market treating the war as an inflation and supply event that forces central banks to stay hawkish, not as a risk-off event that bids refuges, and reporting confirms the mechanism: the oil move lifted the expected global policy path and therefore real yields, while the AI and semiconductor selloff - the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 6.72% in a session - forced margin-driven liquidation of crowded gold longs, which is HSBC Asset Management's reading. Everything on this board follows from that. The currencies that are paid for the barrel led, with AUD up 1.24% on the week, CAD up 0.97% and both scored plus 2. The currencies that pay for it lagged, and the euro area is the extreme case - its October flash PMI fell to a four-month low with S&P Global explicitly blaming rising energy costs and a sharp French contraction, which is the shock arriving as a growth problem rather than as inflation, and it is why the Moody's reprieve on France produced no euro bid. Britain gets the same gas bill but has a central bank 94-97% priced to hike on November 5, and Japan gets the same barrel but has a governor tying rate rises to preventing bond-yield spikes. Switzerland gets neither: a zero policy rate, the lowest ten-year in this file at 0.5030 and an SNB that dropped its increased-willingness language on franc strength in September because haven inflows had receded. In this regime the franc is a funding currency rather than a refuge, which is precisely what Friday showed. The risk to all of this is a single change of state. If Hormuz moves from premium to closure, the supply shock becomes a global growth shock: real yields fall, central banks stop being able to tighten into it, and gold, the franc and the yen are bid together while the commodity-currency leadership and the equity shorts reverse at once. That is one headline away in either direction, which is why conviction is placed on the pairs where a second, scheduled catalyst does the work - the Bank of Canada on Wednesday, Australian CPI thirty minutes before the RBNZ, the Lagarde press conference on Thursday - rather than on the oil premium itself.
